words.definition: Showing care for the needs of other people.

words.definition: A particular way of considering something.

words.definition: A result caused by an action or event.

words.definition: To examine something carefully to understand it.

words.definition: To expect something and prepare for it.

words.definition: Something accepted as true without enough proof.

words.definition: To work with others on a shared task.

words.definition: An agreement in which each side gives up part of what it wants.

words.definition: Acting or happening in a similar way over time.

words.definition: To judge the quality or value of something.

books.title: Speak Your Mind
books.subtitle: Ideas worth sharing
books.description: Express your opinions clearly and thoughtfully through discussion prompts and speaking tasks.

lessons.title: Make your point
lessons.description: Share an opinion and support it with a reason.

sections.title: Say what you think
sections.body: Try phrases such as 'In my view', 'I would argue that', and 'From my perspective'. Then give a clear reason. 'In my view, reading fiction is valuable because it helps us understand other people.'

sections.title: Disagree thoughtfully
sections.body: Show that you heard the other person's idea. 'I see your point, but I think...' or 'That is an interesting argument. Have you considered...?' A good discussion helps both people learn.

lessons.question: Which phrase introduces a respectful disagreement?
options: I see your point, but I think...
lessons.explanation: Acknowledging the other person's point helps keep the discussion respectful.

lessons.title: An argument with support
lessons.description: Connect a claim to evidence and an explanation.

sections.title: Find the parts
sections.body: A claim states an idea. Evidence supports it. An explanation shows why that evidence matters. 'The library should open later' is a claim. A record of evening visits could provide evidence. An explanation could be 'Many visits happen after 6 p.m., so evening opening would suit students who work or study late.'

sections.title: Test the connection
sections.body: Ask whether the evidence actually supports the claim. A personal preference is not enough to show what everyone needs. Look for an assumption between the evidence and the conclusion. Discuss what extra information would make the argument more convincing.

lessons.question: Which detail best supports a claim that students need later library hours?
options: A survey shows many students cannot visit before closing time.
lessons.explanation: The survey connects students' availability directly to the proposed opening hours.

lessons.title: Leave room for uncertainty
lessons.description: Use cautious language when evidence is limited.

sections.title: Match confidence to evidence
sections.body: Words such as may, appears, and suggests help you avoid claiming more than you know. 'The new timetable may improve attendance.' 'These results suggest that shorter sessions help.' Cautious wording makes the degree of certainty clear.

sections.title: Keep the useful detail
sections.body: Caution should not make your message vague. Say what happened and what remains uncertain. 'Attendance rose this month, but we need more evidence before drawing a conclusion.' Practise describing a small classroom survey without assuming it represents everyone.

lessons.question: Which sentence best matches limited evidence from one small class?
options: Every student learns faster in the morning.
The results prove that mornings are always better.
The results suggest that this class may benefit from morning sessions.
lessons.explanation: Suggest and may reflect the limited evidence, and this class keeps the claim appropriately narrow.
